name: Rheem
description: Rheem Mark VII combo organ listing copy. Sourced primarily from combo-organ.com's dedicated Rheem page, which includes firsthand history and design detail directly from Doug Moore, the Mark VII's original designer, cross-referenced against Wikipedia/Reverb summaries. The Kee Bass (a monophonic pedal-bass accessory, not a true combo organ) is out of scope since it's not part of the live catalog. Only one model is documented, so this tree has a single leaf.

nodes.label: Rheem Mark VII
nodes.copy:
Every Rheem Mark VII we restore for sale goes through the same meticulous process we're known for, with dozens of hours devoted to bringing each instrument to exceptional playing condition. We prioritize period-correct vintage components whenever possible, and turn to the best available reproduction parts when originals are no longer viable — always working to preserve the instrument's original character and tone. The result is an organ that plays and sounds better than it likely has in decades.

Yes, that Rheem — better known for water heaters and air conditioners. The Mark VII came out of an odd corner of the company's history: Rheem had acquired an electronics manufacturer built around importing Japanese-made audio gear, and a manager pushed to get into the music instrument business, landing engineer Doug Moore (hired to design guitar amps) the job of turning a disappointing batch of Japanese combo organ prototypes into something worth selling. The result, manufactured for Rheem in Japan by Nakane Denki Co. (with keyboards supplied by Tahachiko, the same company making them for Yamaha at the time), listed for $660 in 1967 and was well-received enough that it reportedly outplayed the competition at the Los Angeles Teen Fair that year. It was also sold through Carvin as an authorized reseller in 1969, and rebadged and sold under the "Barclay" name. It's a five-octave organ offering four voices — Flute, String, Brass and Reed — across three footages (16', 8', 4'), with the Voice and Footage tabs working together similar to a Vox Continental (you need at least one of each engaged to get any sound). It has a genuinely versatile two-octave bass section: a Solo Bass tab that routes the bass voice to its own output jack instead of the main one, Single- and Two-Octave Bass tabs, and a Fuzz Bass tab that adds grit to just the bass voice. Rounding it out are a wide-range Vibrato control, a Mellow/Bright tone switch, and a "Multi-Tone Booster" tab — added mainly because a manager wanted a feature to match Farfisa's Compact line, and which works by rerouting high frequencies around the expression pedal so the pedal shifts from a volume control to more of a tone control when engaged.

Features:
- Cleaned, Lubricated & Restored Key Contacts and Switches
- Addressed Known Resistor Insulation Wear on Tone Generator Boards
- New Electrolytic Capacitors
- Restored/Replaced Optical Volume Pedal
- Fully Restored Power Supply
- CEPCo's Expert Tuning & Voicing Setup
- Cleaned All Tabs, Levers, Switches & Connectors
- All Voltages Checked & Calibrated for Optimum Performance
- New Cables
